activities.title: Choose a safe next step
activities.accessNote: Free, no account or installation. Works offline after MyDay is cached.
activities.instruction: Make four decisions about a fictional training lab. Explain one decision, then check the feedback.
steps: Read the stated permission in each scenario.
Choose the next action using only that permission.
Record why you chose an action. Submit even if you are uncertain; you can retry afterwards.
evidence: One decision and the permission or boundary that supports it.
activities.boundary: Fictional scenarios only; this activity does not connect to any systems.

activities.title: Repair a small network
activities.accessNote: Free, no account or installation. A local simulation, not a real network tool.
activities.instruction: A simulated laptop cannot reach a training website. Trace the failure, change the configuration and test your explanation.
steps: Choose a DNS, routing or firewall fault.
Run the connection test once, then change one setting and run it again.
Record which change helped, why it helped, and what this simplified model cannot prove.
evidence: The failure you observed and the setting you changed.
Why reaching a website does not prove the network is secure.
activities.boundary: All packets and hosts are imaginary. No network traffic is sent.

activities.title: Investigate a sign-in timeline
activities.accessNote: Free, no account. Uses the curriculum's small synthetic log file.
activities.instruction: Inspect the supplied sign-in events. Separate invalid and duplicate rows before making a claim about the activity.
steps: Inspect the raw rows; filtering changes the view only, not the questions' dataset.
Treat a row as valid only when all six fields are present, the timestamp parses and the result is success or failure. Deduplicate valid rows by event ID.
Count valid unique events and failures. Identify a pattern worth checking without calling it a confirmed compromise.
evidence: Relevant event IDs, your hypothesis and one alternative explanation.
A source of additional evidence you would request.
activities.boundary: Made-up training data only; this is a parsing exercise, not a realistic detection benchmark.

activities.title: TryHackMe: start and stop a training lab
activities.accessNote: Sign-in required. Public room instructions checked; signed-in machine allowances were not tested. Use the free alternative if access is restricted.
activities.instruction: Complete Task 1 of the Tutorial room and practise ending your lab session.
steps: Read the room instructions and identify the training machine assigned to you.
Follow Task 1 to open the lab with the provided browser environment. Work only inside that assigned instance.
End the training machine when finished. Return here to record the setup and any access problems.
evidence: Which training environment you used and how you ended it.
One boundary you would check before starting another lab. No flags, passwords or tokens.
activities.boundary: Only the training instance assigned by this room.

activities.title: TryHackMe: network identities and ping
activities.accessNote: Free-account route, subject to current room access. Public instructions checked; authenticated access was not tested. A free in-app alternative is provided.
activities.instruction: Work through Tasks 1–4 in What is Networking?, including the browser simulations in Tasks 3 and 4.
steps: Read Tasks 1 and 2 and sketch the relationship between a local network and the Internet.
In Task 3, compare device addresses and use the room's own browser exercise.
In Task 4, complete the ping simulation on the room's virtual site; explain what a reply demonstrates and what it does not.
evidence: Tasks attempted, your address comparison and an explanation of a ping result.
Describe observations in your own words; keep challenge flags on the provider's site.
activities.boundary: Only the simulations supplied inside the room.

activities.title: Ubuntu: navigate a practice folder
activities.accessNote: Free reading, no account. Hands-on work needs a Linux shell you control; use a disposable practice directory.
activities.instruction: Use the tutorial's directory and file sections to create a small, disposable workspace and navigate it.
steps: Read the sections about opening a terminal, changing directories, and creating folders and files.
Inside a new practice folder you own, create two subfolders and a text note. Move between them and show your current path.
Read the note using the shell. Explain the difference between a relative path and an absolute path using your own folder names.
evidence: Three commands with their observed outputs, redacting your home-directory name if needed.
Your own pair of relative and absolute paths.
activities.boundary: Only a disposable folder on your own machine or assigned Linux lab; no system changes.

activities.title: TryHackMe: first Linux commands
activities.accessNote: Sign-in and a room machine are needed. Public instructions checked; current machine limits were not tested. Try the Ubuntu exercise if blocked.
activities.instruction: Complete Tasks 3–6 in Linux Fundamentals Part 1 after reading its introductory material.
steps: Start the assigned Linux environment in Task 3.
Use Tasks 4 and 5 to practise displaying text, identifying your user, navigating and reading files.
In Task 6, search the supplied files. Explain one search you used, then terminate the machine.
evidence: Task numbers completed or where you stopped, plus three commands and what each showed.
One mistaken assumption you corrected. Do not copy flags or credentials into MyDay.
activities.boundary: Only the Linux machine assigned by this room.

activities.title: OverTheWire: connect and read your first file
activities.accessNote: Free training service with supplied game credentials; no personal account. Requires an SSH client and a network that permits the connection.
activities.instruction: Follow Bandit Level 0 to connect, then the Level 0 → Level 1 page to find the first training file.
steps: Use the host, port and game account given on the Level 0 page.
Follow the site's next-level link. Inspect the starting directory and read the named file.
Use the result only inside the game, then disconnect. Explain why the SSH port must be supplied.
evidence: Your connection method and the commands used to locate the file; omit all passwords and flags.
activities.boundary: Only the game account and actions described by the current Bandit level.

activities.title: Python: classify a short event list
activities.accessNote: Free documentation; no account. Running code needs a local Python 3 installation or an existing training environment.
activities.instruction: Read the chapter's conditionals, loops and functions sections, then write your own tiny event counter.
steps: Create a list containing success, failure, failure and unknown.
Write a function that counts failures without treating unknown as success.
Test an empty list and a list with no failures. Predict each result before running it.
evidence: Your function or a file reference, expected versus actual outputs, and a corrected bug or edge case.
activities.boundary: Only made-up strings in your own script; no accounts or network calls.

activities.title: Git: record and inspect a small change
activities.accessNote: Free online book; no account or hosting service needed. Requires local Git for the exercise.
activities.instruction: Use a new throwaway repository to practise reviewing and committing a text change.
steps: Read the chapter's status, staging and diff sections.
In a new practice repository, add a short README and inspect the change before staging and committing it.
Edit one sentence. Compare the unstaged and staged differences, then write a second descriptive commit.
evidence: The two commit summaries and your explanation of working files, staging and history.
activities.boundary: A disposable repository containing no credentials or personal files; no remote push needed.

activities.title: MDN: annotate a request and response
activities.accessNote: Free reading and a paper or notebook exercise; no account or installation.
activities.instruction: Read MDN's HTTP overview and annotate your own fictional exchange between a browser and a server.
steps: Find the discussion of clients, servers, requests and responses.
Write an invented GET request for /training and a successful response. Label the method, path, status, headers and body.
Explain what would differ for a missing page and why a successful status alone says nothing about authorisation.
evidence: Your annotated exchange and one thing HTTP does not prove about the user.
activities.boundary: Invented messages only; do not record real cookies or authorisation headers.

activities.title: Microsoft Learn: inspect your PowerShell environment
activities.accessNote: Free reading, no account. The exercise needs an existing PowerShell installation; no paid cloud sandbox.
activities.instruction: Use the getting-started chapter to identify your PowerShell edition and distinguish it from other terminals.
steps: Read the chapter's console and version guidance.
In your own non-administrator PowerShell session, inspect $PSVersionTable.
Record the edition and version, explain what a terminal hosts, and name a task that does not require administrator access.
evidence: Edition, version and a short explanation in your own words. No machine name or account name needed.
activities.boundary: Read-only inspection of your own shell; no changes to execution policy or system settings.

activities.title: PortSwigger: investigate a product-filter flaw
activities.accessNote: Free Academy lab; an account can retain progress. Use the lab's instructions and free Community Edition tools if needed.
activities.instruction: Complete the Academy's introductory product-filter SQL injection lab on your assigned instance.
steps: Read the lab objective and open the training instance supplied by the Academy.
Compare a normal product-filter response with your controlled test; attempt the objective before reading a solution.
Record the observed difference and describe a parameterised-query defence. If you used a solution, declare it below.
evidence: The lab status you observed, a redacted before/after comparison and a proposed regression test.
activities.boundary: Only the disposable Academy instance opened from this lab page.

activities.title: PortSwigger: trace reflected browser input
activities.accessNote: Free Academy lab; an account can retain progress. No paid subscription needed for this assignment.
activities.instruction: Complete the introductory reflected-input lab and explain the boundary between text and executable page content.
steps: Launch the lab's own instance and inspect how the search input appears in its response.
Attempt the lab objective using only your assigned instance and your own browser.
Explain the missing output protection and write a defensive regression-test idea.
evidence: The lab status and where input appeared, plus your proposed defence. Record any hints used.
activities.boundary: Only your Academy lab instance. Do not send links or payloads to other people.

activities.title: PortSwigger: check an admin access boundary
activities.accessNote: Free Academy lab; an account can retain progress. No paid subscription needed for this assignment.
activities.instruction: Complete the Academy's unprotected administration lab and explain where the authorisation check should live.
steps: Read the lab objective and open its disposable instance.
Attempt the stated administrative action against the lab's fictional account only.
Record what the server allowed and describe a check that would reject the same request from an ordinary user.
evidence: Observed lab status, the missing control and a negative test using an unauthorised role.
activities.boundary: Only the fictional user and instance named by this Academy lab.
